newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo markets unscathed by bank suspension.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo markets unscathed by bank suspension.

text.p: Tokyo financial markets were unscathed by the news early on Thursday that the Ministry of Finance had suspended most business operations of a regional bank in western Japan.
Brokers said the stock market was already digesting worries over Japan's financial system, so the suspension of Hanwa Bank Ltd was not a bolt from the blue.
The foreign exchange and Japanese government bond markets also reacted calmly to the news, traders said.
Some brokers said the impact was cushioned by the fact Hanwa Bank was a regional bank and not a major one.
"Hanwa is not the first and it probably won't be the last to fail," said Yuichi Matsushita, a senior strategist and general manager at Nikko Research Institute.
"There are still a few smaller banks which could buckle under the weight of bad loans, resulting from the 'bubble' era," he added.
The benchmark 225-share Nikkei average on Tokyo Stock Exchange shrugged off Hanwa in morning trade, gaining 10.58 points or 0.05 percent to 21,200.54 at midday.
The Osaka Securities Exchange banned trade in Hanwa shares for the the entire day.

Problem loans at Hanwa totalled 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion) compared with total capital of 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September, when the bank closed its books for the first half of its business year, the Finance Ministry said.

Share prices for large banks did not flinch but some regional banks prices were dented slightly by the news, brokers added. They said no lasting effect was expected, especially since currencies and bonds were not severely shaken.

"Investors separate good apples from the bad," said Hiroshi Morimoto, Daiwa Securities' general manager. "The news did not discourage them too much because in a way the government is helping them by weeding out companies which are faltering."
News of the suspension did not move the dollar, which was trading in Tokyo near its New York Wednesday close of about 111.50 yen.
"Although traders were relatively cool to the news and talk of Japanese banks' problems, it is not a situation in which to buy the Japanese yen," said a dealer at a European bank.
Traders said early gains in Japanese government bonds on Hanwa Bank's troubles were more than offset by selling from foreign speculative accounts.
The U.S. Treasuries market also disregarded Hanwa's troubles. "The Hanwa news was ignored this morning," a commercial bank trader said.
Stock market sources welcomed news of what was the first such suspension by government regulators in the postwar era.
"Halting business at troubled banks is good because by propping them up hoping they will recover, the problem just grows bigger and bigger," a broker at a "Big Four" securities house said.
Much of Japan's financial system has been dealt a hard blow by the collapse of real estate prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s bubble era, when property and share prices soared.

Hanwa is Japan's third bank failure since World War Two. The two other failures, one last year and one this year, were cleaned up by the creation of new banks to absorb the failed institutions' business.

Hanwa said that in the six months to September 20, it posted a parent current loss of 33.72 billion yen ($303 million) against a profit of 232 million yen ($2.09 million) in the year-ago period. ($1=111 yen)
